children.text: A museum of Philippine military history inside Camp Aguinaldo on EDSA in Quezon City. Opened in 1996, it covers the Army, Navy and Air Force and honors Medal of Valor recipients, while outdoor Kagitingan Park displays retired military equipment. Because it sits inside a military headquarters, you need ID and should confirm access beforehand.

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Museum stands inside Camp Aguinaldo, along EDSA in Quezon City, Metro Manila. Camp Aguinaldo is the general headquarters of the AFP, and the museum is run from the Gen. Arturo Enrile Building within the compound. Pass one checkpoint off the mall-and-skyscraper stretch of EDSA and the atmosphere changes completely. It is one of the few museums where you can calmly take in modern Philippine history and the story of its military.

The museum began in November 1996 on the verbal order of then Chief of Staff Gen. Arturo Enrile. The following year a private nonprofit, the AFP Museum and Historical Library Foundation, was formed to keep it running. That makes it less a facility operated directly by the military than a museum run by a foundation inside a military compound, with regular project support from a veterans' affairs agency. A 2016 news report also described a period when it was in danger of closing for lack of funds.

The building has two floors. The lower level shows how the Philippine military developed through different eras, and the upper level introduces the Army, the Navy (including the Marine Corps) and the Air Force separately. Next to the building, Kagitingan Park displays retired military vehicles and weapons outdoors, which makes it a pleasant walk with children too. Notable holdings include two letters from Apolinario Mabini to Emilio Aguinaldo about Antonio Luna, and Aguinaldo's rayadillo uniform.

What sets this museum apart is that it goes beyond looking at weapons and tells where the Philippine military began. According to Quezon City's public listing, its roots trace back to the Tejeros Convention, where revolutionaries united against Spanish colonial rule. Following the paintings, dioramas, uniforms and weapons, you see the flow of the Philippine military from the revolution through World War II to today. It suits military history fans, and also anyone tired of the usual Manila sightseeing who wants something different. On December 20, 2024, at the AFP's 89th anniversary event, the President announced the relaunch of the renovated museum. Coverage at the time said only that it would open to the public soon and gave no specific date, so please confirm by phone or email whether it is open and when before you go.

The lower level walks you in order through the eras the Philippine military has lived through. Paintings and dioramas explain its roots in the revolutionary forces that rose against Spanish colonial rule.

blocks.title: Army, Navy and Air Force (upper floor)

children.text: The upper level is divided into the Army, the Navy (including the Marine Corps) and the Air Force. Comparing uniforms, weapons and memorabilia branch by branch gives a quick sense of how the Philippine military is organized.
Two letters from Apolinario Mabini to Emilio Aguinaldo about Antonio Luna, and Aguinaldo's rayadillo uniform, are known to be in the collection. Don't miss them if you like stories of the revolution.
A display wall honors recipients of the Medal of Valor. Unveiled in 2011 by former President Fidel Ramos, it lets you read short accounts of soldiers who risked their lives in battle.

The park beside the building holds retired military vehicles and weapons. Reports have mentioned a US M2 105mm howitzer, a Huey helicopter, an M41 light tank and an F-86D Sabre jet, but check on site for what is actually on display.
The collection runs from Katipunan-era weapons to firearms and uniforms of World War II. Equipment such as twin Oerlikon 20mm cannon and a Mark 44 torpedo is also known to be on display.
Coverage of the relaunch listed old rifles and pistols and bladed weapons from Mindanao among the exhibits, a window into regional weapon traditions.
After your visit there is a shop selling books and souvenirs about military history. The stock and hours vary, so treat it as a quick browse, and bring a little cash for any purchase.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: The museum and nearby historic sites

children.text: Show your ID at the Camp Aguinaldo entrance gate and state the purpose of your visit. Bags and vehicles are checked, so arrive with time to spare.
On the ground floor of the Arturo Enrile Building, follow the military history exhibits from the revolution to the present.
Go upstairs to the Army, Navy and Air Force exhibits and the Medal of Valor wall. Take photos only in permitted areas, and ask staff if you are unsure.
Step out to Kagitingan Park and look over the helicopters, tanks and cannon on outdoor display. Earlier is better to avoid the midday heat.
Take a taxi or Grab to the shopping area across EDSA for lunch. Don't count on getting a meal inside the museum.
If you have time, head toward the nearby EDSA People Power Monument and see the site of the 1986 People Power Revolution.
Opening hours and accessible areas can change, so check the latest announcement before you go.
Pass the gate and arrive at the museum. Right after opening there are few visitors, so photos are easier too.
Skim the ground-floor exhibits quickly and look first for key items such as Mabini's letters and Aguinaldo's uniform.
On the upper floor, read a few of the recipient accounts on the Medal of Valor wall.
Finish by looking at the helicopters and tanks in Kagitingan Park.
This is an example for a tight schedule. Adjust it to conditions on the day.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to Quezon City, a taxi or Grab takes around
1 hour
, though traffic can change this a lot.
From Makati, Ortigas, BGC and elsewhere in Manila, you travel along EDSA. Buses, jeepneys and the MRT-3 all run along EDSA, so it is easy to get to a nearby station or stop and switch to a Grab.
Camp Aguinaldo is on EDSA and borders Bonny Serrano Avenue and White Plains Avenue. Ask the museum (8912-7664) before you leave which gate to use.
The exact walking route and gate lack reliable sources, so confirm them locally.
Enter Camp Aguinaldo along with the museum name as your destination. The driver will check at the gate whether the car can enter deeper into the compound.
EDSA is very congested at rush hour, so aim for around 10 a.m. or between 2 and 4 p.m. on a weekday.
Expect a vehicle check and an ID check at the gate. Follow local staff directions on where and whether you can park.
The museum is known to open on weekday daytime hours and is listed as closed on weekends. So the day of the week is fixed first, and the weather is what you choose within that.
To see the outdoor displays at Kagitingan Park, a dry-season morning before the sun climbs is best. In the rainy season sudden afternoon showers are common, so bring an umbrella.

There are few places to stay near the museum, and most travelers sleep in Makati, Ortigas or BGC and visit as a day trip. Large shopping malls line EDSA near the camp, so simply choose a hotel that is easy to travel from.
Eating inside the military compound is difficult, so plan to eat at a mall before or after your visit. Greenhills and SM Megamall are relatively close, and both offer plenty of dining choices.

The easiest lunch is at the malls and restaurant strips lining EDSA. If you go on to Greenhills after the museum, you can combine local food, street snacks and souvenir shopping in one stop. It is hard to buy food in front of the compound, so bring water and a light snack.
Bring a government-issued ID or your passport. Without ID it is hard to get in.
The museum is listed as open on weekdays only, so don't go on a weekend.
Before leaving, confirm with the museum (8912-7664, afpmuseum@gmail.com) that it is open. Listed opening hours differ from source to source.
You will be walking outdoors at the displays, so bring a hat and water.
Take photos only in permitted areas, and ask staff first if you are unsure.
Pairing Kagitingan Park with the nearby EDSA People Power Monument makes a good half-day.
If you want a guided tour, book in advance.
Some visitors report leaving ID at the gate in exchange for a visitor's pass, so keep the pass safe so you don't lose it.
The Medal of Valor wall rewards slow reading, so allow plenty of time.
When crossing EDSA after your visit, use the footbridge or crossing facilities. Crossing the main road at random is dangerous.
This is a military headquarters, so you cannot enter without ID, and hours and fees differ between listings, so be sure to confirm before you go.
It has not been officially confirmed when the museum opened to the public after the December 2024 relaunch, so an inquiry beforehand is essential.
Opening hours are listed differently, as 9 a.m.–5 p.m., 9 a.m.–6 p.m., or with a lunch closure.
This is a military facility, so follow instructions and do not take photos in areas where photography is prohibited.
EDSA is extremely congested at rush hour.
In the rainy season the outdoor displays can be hard to see.
Inside the compound, stay on designated paths and in designated areas and cooperate with the guards' directions.
The big flagship park of Quezon City, a good place to continue with a stroll or a meal after the museum. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so check locally.

11 minutes
on foot from the museum.
Across EDSA, inside the Philippine National Police headquarters, is a museum on police history. How to enter needs local confirmation.
A nearby shopping district reachable by taxi, good for combining a meal with shopping.
